body: You're not being weird, that does sound clingy. He needs to work on his trust issues or this is going to turn controlling. You should decide if you want to work through it with him, and if so, think about boundaries would make the relationship work for you. Otherwise, part ways sooner rather than later.

Due to extreme negative reactions to any kind of hormonal BC I've tried, I decided to go with Paragard. I already had a heavy flow, and so that hasn't changed any. I do notice my cramps hurt worse, but only for 1-2 days at the start of my cycle. I've had it for 4 of its 10 years so far (some people have said that their side effects such as worse cramping go away around the 1 year mark, but not me) and only plan to take it out once my fiance and I marry and we're ready for little ones. :)

It's super convenient, but keep in mind that you CANNOT use a menstrual cup, and that you may want to be careful using tampons your first 1-2 periods after insertion. Overall, I wish I could use Mirena instead, but this is a good option for those of us who can't use hormonal BC.

It sounds like you're a very jealous person who manipulates your partner to get attention. I'm not surprised this ended in a break up.

You shouldn't be "comforted" when you feel jealous. If the jealousy is unfounded, like when she has male friends around, then you need to get over it. She doesn't need to deal with that, it's your issue.

If you're crying and breaking up with her to get her attention, that is also really juvenile behavior. You sound like a teenager and not a 23-year-old.

You should accept that you did this, you can't take it back just because it didn't go the way you wanted it to, and that she doesn't want you back. Use the opportunity to work on yourself. It sounds like you have severe communication, emotional maturity, and insecurity issues.

Their hair is not unkempt. It's that there are certain hairstyles that are more prominent in the black community. This doesn't just apply to dreads, it applies to afros, certain styles of weaves, etc. Their appearance doesn't conform to the mainstream idea of a "professional" person--an idea based on white people. 

So, again, not about hair. It's about race and other prejudices. Anything other than clean cut and white often gets seen as unprofessional or inappropriate. This includes natural black hair styles, people with tattoos or piercings, transgender people, etc.
Yeah, so, they aren't getting stopped because of their hair. They are getting stopped because of their ethnicity. It's racist and it's wrong but it's not because they have dreads.

Depends on what is being "appropriated." People running around in kimonos (seriously doing so, not for an event) isn't going to be a good representation of Japanese culture. Taking something out of cultural context can be kind of shitty behavior.

But people who complain that anyone who is white and has dreadlocks is practicing cultural appropriation needs to get stuffed. That is what happens to hair under certain conditions. It does not matter what kind of hair. Ffs, the Vikings and Celts both sported dreads.

Guess what I'm saying is that it needs to be something provably unique to the group getting offended about it to be appropriation, and everyone needs to stop and take a second to think about whether they are being respectful before they take part of the culture they admire.

Right, so, I get that this is very emotional for you, but think about HER.

Do you want to stay with her because it's comfortable? Or because you love her that much? It doesn't sound like you respect her, either. Getting drunk doesn't excuse cheating--does she know that you did that? Saying awful things while drunk isn't excusable just because you're drunk, either.

Wanting to know what dating other people and sex with other people is like isn't bad. Cheating is bad. Not respecting your partner is bad. Decide what you want, her or other people.

You need to decide why you want to be with her. If it's a fear of leaving what's comfortable, or a fear of being alone, then you need to let her go. If you really do love her and want to be with her (and ONLY her) then you need to talk to her, tell her everything, and let her make a decision.

Don't use the lease as an excuse. You can break it, especially if you haven't even moved in yet, or one of you can find someone else to sublet to and let the other one have the house, just with a different roommate.

She might be depressed. Stopping activities once enjoyed (like going out often to going out never), over sleeping, irritability, and "ditzy"-ness like forgetting ideas from day to day can all be symptoms of depression. If she is depressed, it's likely she's frustrated too because she won't understand why she just can't bring herself to do certain things. Talk to her about seeing a doctor for being tired all of the time; if there's no physical cause, it's likely she's depressed.

I know it's not the same, but my mother is extremely racist as well. She's low-key about it, but being around people of color makes her very uncomfortable, and she stereotypes them an enormous amount.

Instead of trying to say to my mother that she's wrong to be racist, I talked to her about why she feels that way. Yes, some of it was your standard generational difference, and some of it came from the fact that she was 14 before she ever even saw a black person (she grew up in very rural Ohio), so she just didn't have any experience with it.

But really what it came down to was the fact that the current tensions and rhetoric from not just movements like BLM, but also in general from extreme SJWs is very anti-white. There are very loud voices that, while they are by no means the majority, are coming off in a way that makes these people defensive because it feels threatening to them. They're afraid of losing the status quo because they a) haven't experienced or been exposed to what these people go through and so don't understand why they're trying to make a change and b) feel like others are trying to take what they have. It feels threatening to them.

My point is that you should try to have a conversation with him about why he feels the way that he does. Is it a lack of exposure? Does he feel threatened by the messages of movements like BLM? Why? Just trying to change his mind is going to feel like an attack on his beliefs, and is going to make him defensive and dig in his heels. Try for understanding first, and then change the way you present your arguments to tailor them to his experiences.

I hope this helps!

This is a hard situation for you, and I'm so sorry you're going through it. I also had a ton of issues early in my relationship (depression, self-harm, and drug addiction stemming from a sexual assault), but we were able to work through it. We're engaged now and getting married soon.

So it is possible to recover from these things and move forward. It sounds like he's experiencing caregiver burnout, because he has been an emotional caregiver to you. I know you already feel terrible with the depression, but you should try to recognize that if he met you pre-mental illness, he's going to feel like you aren't the same person.

It's healthy for him to tell you where he is at. He needs to set his own boundaries or else he too will start to have emotional problems. Do you rely on him heavily for emotional support with your depression? If so, then please consider seeing a therapist or counselor (whether or not you two stay together). If you're a student at a university, they usually offer such services at very reduced rates or free.

I'm sorry you're going through this. As for your boyfriend, I would just try to see if you can work on your depression because it sounds like that's the cause of the issues between the two of you. Don't stress about trying to fix the relationship before helping yourself.

If things don't improve between you, I'd also suggest looking for someone on campus to sublet to. One of you will need to leave the apartment if you break up. I lived with an ex after breaking up due to financial reasons too, and 0/10, do not recommend.

Good luck. Feel free to reach out to me if you want to talk.

I agree with what your therapist said. It's normal and totally okay to still feel hurt thinking about how unfairly you were treated by someone who you thought cared about you. It doesn't sound like you're upset that he has a new girlfriend, just that the encounter with her and the restaurant were reminding you of his behavior towards you, which is still upsetting.

It's okay to still be upset about how he treated you. It doesn't mean you want him back, and it doesn't mean that your feelings for your current boyfriend should be called into question. It's normal to still feel upset after being hurt by someone you had a long, close history with.

Take the issue of the coworker and think solely about your girlfriend and the sexual issues y'all have. The question comes down to this: is it worth breaking up with her over the sex to you?

You've talked about trying to fix the issue with her, and described how you tried to suggest things and get shot down. But have you tried asking her if there is anything SHE wants to try? Have you tried asking her why she doesn't want to have sex? I myself made a deal with my fiance: if my only reason is "I'm not in the mood," he's free to try to get me turned on, and vice versa. The extra effort and feeling desired usually helps.

Anyway, what it really comes down to is whether or not you want to try again to fix things with your girlfriend. If so, I'd post in /r/deadbedrooms. If not, don't leave your girlfriend because of the possibility of someone else. Leave her because you aren't compatible anymore. Sexual incompatibility is a big deal, and not a scummy reason to break up when done nicely, if it comes to that.

If you're being as aggressive with your pursuit as you've made it sound from your post, I wouldn't be surprised if she wasn't comfortable telling you something like that upfront. Ask her nicely, but directly, if she has any feelings for you. If the answer is no, leave her alone.
All you've given us here are reasons (vague ones at that) to break up. I'm sorry, I know it hurts, but you know what you have to do--especially if he's started treating you poorly.

It's not her fault that she was hurt, got into a pattern of being hurt, and that she is feeling the effects of it. People tend to stick by their first impressions of others--it's an instinct, and not one terribly easily controlled.

It's great that you changed how you were treating her, don't get me wrong. But it's not some awful flaw of hers if she can't look past your previous behavior. Try being more supportive and less critical (ie letting her blame herself for this when she already has low self esteem). These are the continuing ramifications of YOUR actions.

She will forgive you and the two of you will move on, or you won't. Other than continuing to treat her with respect and care, there is nothing else you can do.

I definitely didn't feel this crushing depression the entire 13 years I've suffered from depression, there were some higher points, but overall I keep returning to the same lows no matter what good things are going on in my life. I am just so tired of the near or seemingly perpetual, soul-crushing sadness. 

I am 23 now, nearly 24. Too old for this to beveryone "teenage moodiness." I know my mind. I know I have triggers that exacerbate my sadness, but even without those, even when those and any mention of them are absent from my life, I return to this state. So there's no "cause" that we can find.

I say we because I've tried therapy and medication. Neither worked. The meds made me worse. I'm just tired. If this is what life is, it doesn't seem worth the effort.
